title: Energy stores and transfers
ks3: Energy: stores, transfers, conservation, efficiency and resources
intro: Energy is stored in different ways and moves between stores. Practise naming stores and transfers, energy diagrams, efficiency and energy resources.
description: Free KS3 Physics energy questions with answers: energy stores, energy transfers, conservation of energy, efficiency, Sankey diagrams and renewable resources. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: Which energy store does a battery have?
questions.hint: The energy is in the substances inside the battery.
questions.explain: A battery stores energy in a chemical store. Food and fuels have chemical stores too.

questions.q: A ball is held high above the ground. Which store has energy because of its height?
questions.hint: If you let go, gravity pulls it down.
questions.explain: Objects that are lifted up have energy in their gravitational store. The higher they are, the more energy.

questions.q: A car speeds up. Which store increases?
questions.hint: This store is about movement.
questions.explain: The kinetic store is the energy an object has because it is moving. Faster means more kinetic energy.

questions.q: A stretched rubber band stores energy in which store?
questions.hint: Think of things that are stretched or squashed.
questions.explain: Stretched or squashed objects, like rubber bands and springs, have energy in an elastic store.

questions.q: A hot cup of tea has lots of energy in which store?
questions.hint: Hotter things have more energy in this store.
questions.explain: The hot tea has energy in its thermal store. As it cools down, energy moves to the thermal store of the room.

questions.q: The Sun gives out huge amounts of energy. Which store does this energy come from?
questions.hint: Deep inside the Sun, the tiny centres of atoms join together.
questions.explain: Reactions in the centres (nuclei) of atoms in the Sun's core release energy from the nuclear store. It reaches us as light and other radiation.

questions.q: A bungee jumper reaches the very bottom of the jump and is still for a moment. Which store has the most energy now?
options: The elastic store of the stretched cord
The kinetic store of the jumper
The gravitational store of the jumper
The chemical store of the cord
questions.hint: At the bottom the jumper is not moving, and is as low as they go. What is stretched as far as it can be?
questions.explain: At the bottom the jumper is still (kinetic store empty) and at the lowest point (gravitational store as low as it gets). The energy is now in the elastic store of the stretched cord, which then pulls the jumper back up.

questions.q: A ball falls from a shelf. Energy is transferred from…
options: the gravitational store to the kinetic store
the kinetic store to the gravitational store
the chemical store to the thermal store
the elastic store to the kinetic store
questions.hint: As it falls it gets lower and faster.
questions.explain: Getting lower empties the gravitational store, and getting faster fills the kinetic store.

questions.q: You rub your hands together quickly. Your hands get warm. Energy goes into which store?
questions.hint: Warmer things have more of this store.
questions.explain: Friction between your hands transfers energy to the thermal store of your hands, so they warm up.

questions.q: Which device is mainly designed to transfer energy electrically to a kinetic store?
questions.hint: Which one makes something move?
questions.explain: A fan's motor makes the blades spin: that is a kinetic store. A kettle and a toaster heat things (thermal) and a bulb gives out light.

questions.q: A charger cable carries energy from the wall socket to a phone battery. How is the energy transferred?
questions.hint: What flows along the cable?
questions.explain: The energy is transferred electrically, by an electric current in the cable. It ends up in the chemical store of the phone's battery.

questions.q: A child on a swing goes from the lowest point up to the highest point. Energy is transferred from…
options: the kinetic store to the gravitational store
the gravitational store to the kinetic store
the elastic store to the chemical store
the thermal store to the kinetic store
questions.hint: On the way up, the swing slows down and gets higher.
questions.explain: Slowing down empties the kinetic store, and getting higher fills the gravitational store. On the way back down it happens the other way round.

questions.q: You wind up a toy car, which squashes a spring inside it, then let it go. Which energy transfer happens as the car moves off?
questions.hint: Winding it up squashes the spring. What happens to the spring when you let go?
questions.explain: Winding the car fills the elastic store of the spring. When you let go, the spring unwinds and energy moves to the kinetic store of the car.

questions.q: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. So what happens to it?
options: It is transferred from one store to another
It gets used up and disappears
questions.hint: This is called the law of conservation of energy.
questions.explain: Energy is never made or destroyed: it only moves between stores. When energy seems "used up", it has usually spread out as heat.

questions.q: A motor is given 500 J of energy. It transfers 350 J usefully to a kinetic store. How much energy is wasted?
questions.hint: Energy in = useful energy + wasted energy.
questions.explain: 500 J − 350 J = 150 J is wasted, mostly heating the motor and its surroundings.

questions.q: This diagram is for an old filament light bulb. Which energy is wasted?
questions.hint: What is a light bulb for?
questions.explain: A bulb is for giving light, so the light (20 J) is useful and the 80 J that heats the room is wasted.

questions.q: Use the diagram. What is the efficiency of this light bulb, as a percentage?
questions.hint: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in.
questions.explain: Efficiency = 20 J ÷ 100 J = 0.2 = 20%.

questions.q: An LED bulb gives out 45 J of light for every 50 J of electrical energy put in. What is its efficiency as a percentage?
questions.hint: Divide useful energy by total energy, then change to a percentage.
questions.explain: 45 ÷ 50 = 0.9 = 90%. LED bulbs waste much less energy than filament bulbs.

questions.q: An electric kettle is used to boil water. Which energy transfer is the useful one?
options: Heating the air around the kettle
The sound of the water bubbling
Light from the little lamp on the switch
questions.hint: What do you want the kettle to do?
questions.explain: A kettle is for heating water, so energy going to the thermal store of the water is useful. Heating the air and the noise are wasted.

questions.q: A ball is dropped. Each bounce is lower than the one before. What has happened to the energy?
options: It has been transferred to thermal stores of the ball and the floor, and to the air as sound
It has been destroyed each time the ball hits the floor
It has been used up by gravity
It has turned into new air particles
questions.hint: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. Listen and feel: what happens each time the ball hits the floor?
questions.explain: Energy is conserved. At each bounce some energy is transferred by sound and heats the ball, the floor and the air a tiny bit. Less energy is left, so the ball cannot get as high. The energy has spread out, so it is hard to use again.

questions.q: This energy diagram is for a TV. What is the efficiency of the TV, as a percentage?
questions.hint: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in. Then change to a percentage.
questions.explain:
A TV is for light and sound, so 60 J is useful.
Efficiency = 60 J ÷ 200 J = 0.3 = 30%. The other 140 J heats the TV and the room.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
questions.hint: Renewable resources will not run out.
questions.explain: Wind will keep blowing, so it is renewable. Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels: they will run out.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-renewable energy resource?
questions.hint: Which one took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced?
questions.explain: Natural gas is a fossil fuel. It took millions of years to form, and once burned it is gone.

questions.q: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide. Why is this a problem?
options: It uses up the oxygen in the oceans
questions.hint: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas.
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere, which adds to global warming and climate change. (The ozone layer is damaged by other gases, not carbon dioxide.)

questions.q: Which energy resource does not depend on the weather?
questions.hint: Which one uses heat from deep inside the Earth?
questions.explain: Geothermal power uses heat from underground rocks, which is there whatever the weather. Wind and solar change from day to day, and hydroelectric needs rain to fill the reservoirs.

questions.q: Which energy resource uses sunlight to make electricity?
questions.hint: Which one has the Sun in its name?
questions.explain: Solar panels (solar cells) transfer energy from sunlight straight into electricity. Solar power is renewable.

questions.q: Why can't a country get all of its electricity from wind turbines alone?
options: The wind does not always blow, so it is not always reliable
Wind turbines make too much carbon dioxide
The wind will run out one day
Wind turbines only work at night
questions.hint: Think about a calm, still day.
questions.explain: On calm days the turbines stop, so there is little or no electricity from them. So other resources, or ways of storing energy, are needed as well. Wind is renewable and does not give out carbon dioxide while it works.

questions.q: Wood is burned as a fuel in some stoves. Why is wood called a renewable resource?
options: New trees can be grown to replace the ones cut down
Burning wood does not give out any carbon dioxide
questions.hint: Can we make more of it in a human lifetime?
questions.explain: Trees grow in a few years or tens of years, so we can plant more to replace the wood we burn. Fossil fuels take millions of years to form. Burning wood still gives out carbon dioxide.
